entries.match_title: Faster! Louder! Brighter! How the attention economy overwhelmed children’s TV - The Guardian
entries.canonical_title: Faster! Louder! Brighter! How the attention economy overwhelmed children’s TV
entries.source_verification: Original Guardian long read, September 17, 2026; originally published in Aeon as The bombarding of childhood
entries.preview: The pace of children's screen media matters beyond minutes watched: rapid cuts and repeated rewards can interrupt opportunities to reflect, infer, and absorb a story. Slow is not inherently better; the key is whether a child has time to make meaning.

editorial_notes.argument: Media quality cannot be reduced to screen-time totals or educational subject matter. Kucirkova argues that the rhythm of children's media shapes opportunities to reflect, understand a story and connect emotionally: constantly shifting cues may capture attention while leaving too little space to process.
editorial_notes.design_relevance: The relevant design question for focus interventions is not simply how long someone looks at a screen, but whether the interface permits uninterrupted interpretation, deliberate pauses, repetition and self-directed attention. This application to AI tools is a design implication, not a measured AI outcome.
editorial_notes.caveat: This is a research-informed essay drawing on children's media comparisons and the Kids' Slow Media Project, not an experiment showing that all fast-paced media harms children or that slower media always produces better learning.
